# Results — Study 163 (Friday-13th) on real ^GSPC tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Signal: the daily
close-to-close log-return of the S&P 500 (^GSPC) on every Friday-the-13th since
1928-01-03, tested against all other Fridays and against a Friday-the-6th placebo.
As-of **2026-06-15**.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | n trading days | n Friday-13ths | Fingerprint |
|---|---|--:|--:|---|
| ^GSPC (shared cache) | 1928-01-03 → 2026-06-12 | 24,728 | 168 | `df3897aef897` |

## The honest test — Friday-13th vs all other Fridays

**Primary result: the 13th is unremarkable.**

| Group | n | mean return (bps/day) | HAC t-stat | Welch p-value |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Friday-the-13th** | 168 | **+6.90** | +0.57 | — |
| All other Fridays | 4,776 | +4.60 | — | — |
| **Contrast (13th minus rest)** | — | **+2.30** | — | **0.8162** |

- The Friday-13th mean is **+6.90 bps/day** vs +4.60 bps for other Fridays — the
  13th is actually *above* average, and the difference is statistically
  **indistinguishable from zero** (Welch p = 0.82, HAC t = +0.57 on the 13th alone).
- **Effective n = 168 events** over 99 years (~1.7/year). Even at this long horizon
  the sample is too thin to detect anything smaller than a very large effect.

## The placebo — Friday-the-6th

| Group | n | mean return (bps/day) | Contrast vs other Fridays | p-value |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Friday-the-6th** | 168 | **+8.59** | **+4.04 bps** | **0.6624** |

Friday-the-6th also outperforms the Friday average, by 4 bps, and also insignificantly.
Both the "superstitious" and the "control" day look almost identical. The 13th has
no special claim to anomalous status.

## Multiple comparisons — all four "special Friday" day-of-month slots

Fridays fall on the 6th, 13th, 20th, or 27th of any month. Testing all four and
picking the most extreme without correction would inflate the false-positive rate
fourfold. We report the raw p-values *and* the Bonferroni-corrected p (k=4):

| Day of month | n | mean (bps/day) | Contrast vs rest | Raw p | Bonferroni p |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **27th** | 167 | **−16.10** | **−21.51** | **0.0109** | **0.0438** |
| 20th | 168 | −8.24 | −13.37 | 0.0978 | 0.3911 |
| 6th | 168 | +8.59 | +4.04 | 0.6624 | 1.0000 |
| **13th** | 168 | **+6.90** | **+2.30** | **0.8162** | **1.0000** |

Friday-the-27th has the *lowest* raw p (0.011) — it barely survives Bonferroni at
the 0.05 level (corrected p = 0.044). The 13th has the **highest** p of the four
(0.82). If superstition predicted anything, it got the wrong slot.

## Sub-period: the Kolb & Rodriguez (1987) era

Kolb & Rodriguez found a negative effect in the Dow Jones Industrial Average from
1940 to 1987. On the S&P 500 in the same era:

| Era | n Friday-13ths | Contrast (bps) | Welch t | p-value |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1940–1987 (K&R era) | 82 | +2.18 | +0.28 | 0.781 |
| 1988–2026 (post-pub) | 64 | +21.27 | +1.04 | 0.302 |
| **Full sample 1928–2026** | **168** | **+2.30** | **+0.23** | **0.816** |

Even within the original authors' own era the GSPC shows no negative effect. The
discrepancy with their paper likely reflects the different index (DJIA vs S&P 500)
and their smaller 1940-only starting window.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** Friday-13th mean return +6.90 bps vs +4.60 bps for other
  Fridays; contrast +2.30 bps, Welch p = 0.82, HAC t = +0.57. Completely
  indistinguishable from noise. Bonferroni-corrected p = 1.00. Not even the most
  extreme of the four "special Friday" slots — that dubious honour belongs to
  Friday-the-27th (raw p = 0.011, Bonferroni p = 0.044).
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** There is no directional signal here, so the question
  of tradability does not arise. Even if the effect were real, with ~1.7 events
  per year the strategy would take decades to accumulate meaningful evidence, and
  any execution cost would trivially exceed a 2 bps/day premium measured with
  p = 0.82.
- **Superstition vs data — BUSTED.** Friday-13th is, on average, a very slightly
  *above*-average trading day. The fear is not just uncorrelated with the data —
  it points in the wrong direction.
